title: Element-Wise Femoral Stress Prediction: A Hybrid Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Finite Element Analysis
authors: Sikha O K, Abdollah Moslemi, Elham Alizadeh, Ludovic Humbert, Miguel A. Gonzalez Ballester, Jerome Noailly
abstract: Hip fractures represent a significant clinical challenge because they cause excess disability and mortality, and have a growing incidence in aging populations, as bone fragility increases. Although finite element analysis (FEA) provides biomechanical assessment of femoral strength, its clinical applicability is mainly limited by high computational cost. Conventional machine learning (ML) approaches have been explored as surrogate models for FEA; predictions are fast but fail to capture the spatial and topological structure of finite element meshes. To address these limitations, this study proposes a hybrid Graph Neural Network (GNN)-based framework for femoral stress prediction using graph-structured finite element modeling (FEM) data. The proposed GCN-SAGE-Residual architecture combines graph convolution, neighborhood aggregation, and residual learning to model spatial dependencies and stress propagation across mesh elements. We systematically evaluated 14 models in a primary comparison, spanning classical ML methods and baseline GNN architectures, complemented by a targeted architectural ablation that isolates the contribution of each component of the proposed design. Evaluation results demonstrate that the proposed hybrid architecture achieves the strongest predictive performance among all evaluated models. The proposed hybrid model achieves the best performance with an R^2 score of 0.8022 and mean absolute error of 2.879 MPa, highlighting the importance of incorporating mesh topology in biomechanical prediction tasks. The proposed framework provides a scalable and computationally efficient alternative for FEM-based orthopedic analyses and fracture risk assessment. The code is publicly available on GitHub.

infographic.key_insight: A hybrid GCN-SAGE-Residual network predicts element-wise femoral stress while capturing finite element mesh topology.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The surrogate offers a computationally efficient alternative to femoral FEA, with potential applications in orthopedic analysis and fracture risk assessment.
method: Represent femoral finite element data as graphs.
Combine graph convolution, neighborhood aggregation, and residual learning.
Learn spatial dependencies and stress propagation across mesh elements.
infographic.evidence_signal: The hybrid model performed best in a 14-model comparison, achieving R² = 0.8022 and MAE = 2.879 MPa, with an additional targeted architectural ablation.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish generalization to unseen patient populations, mesh resolutions, or loading conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Element-Wise Femoral Stress Prediction: A Hybrid Graph Neural Network Surrogate for Finite Element Analysis

title: Constitutive Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Finite Element Model Updating: Closed-Form Hyperelastic Strain Energies from Heterogeneous Experiments
authors: Kian P. Abdolazizi, Kevin Linka, Christian J. Cyron
abstract: Calibrating a hyperelastic constitutive model for a soft material traditionally poses two problems: an expert must choose its functional form, and several homogeneous tests must determine its parameters. Neural constitutive models solve the first, but either remain black boxes or draw on a library of candidate terms fixed in advance. Full-field measurements, such as those from digital image correlation (DIC), promise to solve the second, replacing those tests by a single heterogeneous one. Two gaps remain: flexibility during training with interpretability afterwards, and a way to train such a model on one heterogeneous test. Here we close both. We embed a constitutive Kolmogorov-Arnold network (CKAN) in finite element model updating (FEMU) and train it by minimizing the mismatch between the predicted and the measured kinematic fields and reaction forces. Pruning and symbolic regression then reduce the trained network to a compact closed-form strain energy that satisfies every constitutive requirement. On perforated natural-rubber membranes, the CKANs reproduce the DIC displacement fields with median errors between one and two percent, and transfer to a hole pattern withheld from training. On a perforated silicone plate, a CKAN trained on one stretch profile at a single load reproduces that profile and the measured reaction force to within a few percent. On an aortic specimen inflated under pressure, an anisotropic CKAN predicts the inflated three-dimensional shape. The discovered closed-form energies match the CKANs they replace on the training data and can be compared directly with established models.

infographic.key_insight: Constitutive Kolmogorov-Arnold networks embedded in finite element model updating learn hyperelastic behavior from heterogeneous experiments and yield compact, closed-form strain energies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach can reduce reliance on predefined constitutive laws and multiple homogeneous tests while producing interpretable material models for finite element analysis.
method: Embed a constitutive Kolmogorov-Arnold network in finite element model updating.
Fit measured kinematic fields and reaction forces.
Apply pruning and symbolic regression to extract closed-form energies satisfying constitutive requirements.
infographic.evidence_signal: Rubber tests showed median displacement errors of 1–2% and transfer to a withheld hole pattern; silicone predictions matched a measured profile and force within a few percent, while an anisotropic model predicted an inflated aortic specimen’s 3D shape.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer to a withheld geometry is demonstrated, but generalization beyond the measured loading conditions requires further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Constitutive Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in Finite Element Model Updating: Closed-Form Hyperelastic Strain Energies from Heterogeneous Experiments

title: AI agents can redesign engineering parts with more than a thousand CAD parameters and nonlinear simulations
authors: Alexandra Starostina, Alexander Hermann, Mahish Guru, Kartik Bali, Roland Aydin, Christian C. Cyron
abstract: Simulation-driven design of real engineering components has to meet three conditions at once. It runs on few solves, since a nonlinear finite-element simulation of a 3D part takes hours; its design space has many values, the hundreds to thousands of values of the part's CAD model; and a better design often needs a redesign, coordinated changes of the part's proportions rather than local polishing of its surface. Automated optimisers meet at most two of these conditions. Classical optimisers, Bayesian or derivative-free, need a person to cut the design down to a few parameters, and on all the values they need far more solves; industrial shape optimisers move every surface node of the mesh in one solve per cycle, but only in small steps that polish rather than redesign. We ask whether a general-purpose large language model (LLM) can meet all three by joining what it knows with what the simulation shows. GPT-6 Astra edits a magnesium stent through a CAD geometry parametrisation of about 1,650 values, with a budget of 15 simulations; every proposal is built in CAD, meshed and simulated with large-deformation plasticity and contact, and the LLM reads the full results of every solve. Within that budget it lowered the objective, a high percentile of the strains in the stent's bends, by 32%; on the same budget, the industrial shape optimiser Tosca improved the original design by a tenth and then stopped improving. An earlier GPT-6 Astra design, 25% lower in the same objective, was checked in an independent, higher-fidelity model of the full deployment with crimping and damage: it was 14% less strained than the original after the full chain, and its most damaged spot began to fail later and carried 63% less damage at full expansion. LLMs can thus join their learned knowledge with simulation data to adjust more than a thousand design values and reach valid designs with real improvements.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM-guided workflow redesigned a magnesium stent across about 1,650 CAD parameters, reducing a high-percentile bend-strain objective by 32% within 15 nonlinear simulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could enable coordinated component redesign when expensive nonlinear analyses limit the simulation budget.
method: GPT-6 Astra proposed coordinated edits to the stent’s CAD parameters.
Each proposal was built, meshed and simulated with large-deformation plasticity and contact.
The LLM used full simulation results to guide subsequent edits.
infographic.evidence_signal: At the same 15-simulation budget, Tosca achieved roughly 10% improvement; an earlier LLM design independently evaluated through full deployment showed 14% lower strain and 63% less damage at its most damaged spot.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern one stent case, and the independent higher-fidelity validation tested an earlier design rather than the final 32%-improved design.
infographic.paper_title: AI agents can redesign engineering parts with more than a thousand CAD parameters and nonlinear simulations

title: Emergent Fatigue Dynamics from Foundational Interatomic Potentials
authors: Jingye Tan, Benjamin A. Jasperson, Eric Rothchild, Anders Johansson, Rèmi Dingreville, Krishna Garikipati
abstract: Foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials are trained on large, diverse DFT datasets, but their validation rests on equilibrium states, which does not guarantee correct emergent behavior in large-scale molecular dynamics. Where no direct experimental validation is available, comparisons to physically motivated potentials are valuable for drawing insight. We distinguish static properties, which are thermally accessible, from emergent properties, which require work from an external fatigue stress to drive rare events, and compare the potentials on both. An EAM potential and the NequIP foundational potential both agree closely with reference data for many near-equilibrium properties, but NequIP predicts an anomalously low intrinsic stacking fault energy ($\sim7$ times lower than EAM) and thus predicts far more plastic deformation under fatigue cycling of a nanoscale flaw modeled after the classical Griffith crack problem. Per-atom energy distributions after loading show that the two potentials differ most at energies far above what is thermally accessible. We also document memory-related crashes and silent extrapolation as practical concerns for practitioners of these foundational model forms.

infographic.key_insight: Near-equilibrium agreement does not guarantee reliable fatigue dynamics: NequIP predicts much more plastic deformation than EAM under cyclic loading.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fatigue simulations using foundational interatomic potentials need validation of driven, rare-event behavior beyond equilibrium benchmarks.
method: Compare EAM and foundational NequIP potentials on near-equilibrium properties.
Apply fatigue cycling to a nanoscale flaw modeled after a classical Griffith crack.
Examine post-loading per-atom energy distributions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Both potentials closely match reference data for many near-equilibrium properties, but NequIP predicts an intrinsic stacking fault energy about sevenfold lower than EAM, with the largest post-loading energy differences occurring beyond thermally accessible energies.
infographic.watch_item: Without direct experimental validation of fatigue behavior, the comparison is diagnostic rather than definitive; memory-related crashes and silent extrapolation also warrant monitoring.
infographic.paper_title: Emergent Fatigue Dynamics from Foundational Interatomic Potentials

title: Frame Based Inelasticity for Strength and Fracture in Anisotropic Media
authors: Robert Lipton, Prakash K. C.
abstract: A field theory is presented for predicting damage and fracture in brittle materials. Four concepts are used: a new nonlocal deformation gradient for dynamic stress analysis in anisotropic media, a new type of phase field coming from a constitutive law, the evolution of material displacement from Newton's second law, and a new incorporation of scaled strength surfaces into constitutive laws for predicting dynamic and quasi-static fracture patterns. The elastic softening is governed by the strain dynamics through the constitutive law and in this way we provide the two way coupling between strain and fracture. Simulations validating the approach for both dynamic and quasi-static fracture analysis are compared to experimental results and other simulation methods. The model is capable of predicting material strength in titania and the competition between strength and energy in soda lime glass and titana and captures dynamic crack branching in soda lime glass and concrete.

infographic.key_insight: A frame-based nonlocal field theory couples strain and fracture through constitutive softening to predict strength and crack evolution in anisotropic brittle materials.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports dynamic and quasi-static fracture analysis where material strength, fracture energy, and anisotropy influence failure.
method: Use a nonlocal deformation gradient for stress analysis in anisotropic media.
Couple displacement dynamics from Newton’s second law with a constitutively derived phase field.
Embed scaled strength surfaces in constitutive laws to govern softening and fracture.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports comparisons with experiments and other simulations, including strength prediction in titania, strength–energy competition in glass and titania, and dynamic crack branching in glass and concrete.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify calibration requirements, computational cost, or quantitative prediction errors.
infographic.paper_title: Frame Based Inelasticity for Strength and Fracture in Anisotropic Media

title: Unusual increase in electrical and thermal conductivity of severely deformed CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy: Roles of disordering and nanostructuring in electron and phonon transport
authors: Jacqueline Hidalgo-Jiménez, Payam Edalati, Md Amirul Islam, Makoto Arita, Dmitry Chernyshov, Bidyut Baran Saha
abstract: This work investigates how defect engineering and nanostructuring via severe plastic deformation influence electrical and thermal transport in the high-entropy alloy CrMnFeCoNi. High-pressure torsion (HPT) for up to N = 4 turns produces a hierarchical defect structure, including deformation twins at low strains, dislocations and Lomer-Cottrell locks at intermediate strains, and a high fraction of high-angle grain boundaries at large strains. While hardness naturally increases and saturates at ~520 Hv, both electrical and thermal conductivity exhibit an unusual increase upon HPT processing (from 0.953 MS m-1 and 10.3 W m-1 K-1 after homogenization to 1.003 +- 0.005 MS m-1 and 14.4 W m-1 K-1 after N = 4). Analysis based on the Wiedemann-Franz law indicates a modest increase in electron transport (~5%) and a significant increase in phonon transport (~100%) after HPT processing. The phonon mean free path remains small on the order of 0.6-1.1 nm, and comparison with the Cahill-Pohl model shows that heat transport occurs near the minimum thermal conductivity limit, where vibrational modes are strongly scattered. This suggests that the enhancement in thermal transport is not governed by conventional defect scattering, but it is hypothesized that modifications in atomic-scale disorder, such as deformation-induced short-range ordering, are responsible for this unusual behavior. Specific heat capacity increases after HPT, consistent with stored defect energy. The linear thermal expansion exhibits a non-monotonic behavior, decreasing initially due to internal stresses and relaxation effects, and increasing at higher strains due to grain boundary-induced anharmonicity. These findings highlight the complex interplay between defects, atomic-scale disorder, and nanostructure in governing the electrical and thermal properties of severely deformed high-entropy alloys via electron and phonon scattering.

infographic.key_insight: Severe plastic deformation of CrMnFeCoNi increases both electrical and thermal conductivity despite introducing dense defects, with atomic-scale disorder changes proposed as the cause.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Defect engineering may offer a route to combine high hardness with improved charge and heat transport in high-entropy alloys.
method: Apply high-pressure torsion for up to 4 turns to generate hierarchical defects and nanostructure.
Characterize hardness, electrical and thermal transport, heat capacity, and thermal expansion.
Use Wiedemann–Franz analysis and the Cahill–Pohl model to interpret heat transport.
infographic.evidence_signal: After 4 turns, electrical conductivity rises from 0.953 to 1.003 ± 0.005 MS/m and thermal conductivity from 10.3 to 14.4 W/(m·K), with estimated electron and phonon contributions increasing by approximately 5% and 100%, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Deformation-induced short-range ordering remains a hypothesized mechanism rather than an established cause of the transport enhancement.
infographic.paper_title: Unusual increase in electrical and thermal conductivity of severely deformed CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy: Roles of disordering and nanostructuring in electron and phonon transport

title: Ising-Encoded Computational Homogenization: Stress as a Quantum Observable
authors: Mourad Halla, Suvranu De
abstract: Computational homogenization requires repeated solutions of representative volume element (RVE) problems to determine the effective response transferred to the macroscale, including the homogenized stress. Here, we develop a basis-encoded, energy-based variational quantum formulation for linear-elastic computational homogenization. The reduced finite-element energy of the RVE is expressed as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem and mapped to an Ising Hamiltonian, whose ground state represents the equilibrium fluctuation field on the encoding grid. Using the Hellmann--Feynman theorem, differentiation of the strain-dependent Hamiltonian with respect to the prescribed macroscopic strain yields stress observables whose expectation values recover the conventional volume-averaged homogenized stress. A key structural result is that, although the equilibrium Hamiltonian is two-local, the stress observables are one-local. In linear elasticity, the two-qubit coupling coefficients are independent of macroscopic strain, hence, differentiation eliminates all two-qubit coupling terms, leaving only identity and single-qubit Pauli-$Z$ operators. These observables are diagonal in the same computational basis as the Ising Hamiltonian and can therefore be evaluated from the same computational-basis measurements used for the energy. Consequently, the homogenized stress can be obtained directly from the optimized quantum state using the same computational basis measurements as the Ising Hamiltonian, without requiring reconstruction of the microscopic displacement field or an additional measurement basis. Ground states are approximated using the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), and the formulation is demonstrated on a two-dimensional periodic RVE.

infographic.key_insight: For linear-elastic homogenization, stress is a one-local quantum observable obtainable from the same computational-basis measurements as the two-local equilibrium Hamiltonian.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The formulation extracts effective RVE stress for macroscale constitutive calculations without reconstructing the microscopic displacement field or adding a measurement basis.
method: Encode the reduced finite-element RVE energy as a QUBO and map it to an Ising Hamiltonian.
Approximate the equilibrium ground state using the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE).
Differentiate the strain-dependent Hamiltonian via Hellmann–Feynman to obtain stress observables containing only identity and single-qubit Pauli-Z terms.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a demonstration on a two-dimensional periodic RVE and establishes equivalence to conventional volume-averaged stress, but gives no quantitative accuracy or runtime results.
infographic.watch_item: Practical stress accuracy depends on the encoding resolution and VQE state quality; computational advantage is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Ising-Encoded Computational Homogenization: Stress as a Quantum Observable

title: A locking-free enriched linearized neural network for linear elasticity
authors: Bonyong Kim, Young Ju Lee
abstract: Volumetric locking remains a fundamental challenge for neural-network Galerkin methods in nearly incompressible elasticity. We introduce the \emph{locking-free enriched linearized neural network} (LF-ENN), to the best of our knowledge, the first neural-network Galerkin method with a rigorous locking-free guarantee. Building on the enriched Galerkin framework, the method combines neural approximation with a structure-preserving enrichment that reduces the discrete incompressibility constraint to a graph-Laplacian problem. This construction enables divergence-free corrections and error estimates uniform in the Lamé parameter $λ\in(0,\infty]$. Nitsche boundary enforcement and tailored stabilization overcome the lack of conventional finite element trace inequalities for neural trial spaces. Under suitable approximation and mesh-resolution assumptions, we establish stability and error estimates independent of network width, mesh size, and $λ$, including an $O(h^s)$ estimate for reduced-regularity solutions with $s>1/2$. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions confirm locking-free behavior and demonstrate substantial gains in displacement accuracy. In particular, LF-ENN achieves approximately twelve times smaller displacement error than a higher-order locking-free enriched Galerkin method while using fewer than one-third as many unknowns. These results establish a rigorous neural Galerkin framework that combines incompressibility robustness with markedly improved approximation accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: LF-ENN combines neural approximation with structure-preserving enrichment to provide a rigorous locking-free guarantee for nearly incompressible linear elasticity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports accurate displacement prediction as incompressibility increases, without volumetric locking degrading the solution.
method: Enriches a linearized neural trial space to reduce discrete incompressibility constraints to a graph-Laplacian problem.
Constructs divergence-free corrections with error estimates uniform in the Lamé parameter λ.
Uses Nitsche boundary enforcement and tailored stabilization for neural trial spaces.
infographic.evidence_signal: In 2D and 3D numerical experiments, LF-ENN demonstrates locking-free behavior; a reported comparison achieves approximately 12× smaller displacement error than a higher-order locking-free enriched Galerkin method with fewer than one-third as many unknowns.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees require suitable approximation and mesh-resolution assumptions; fewer unknowns alone does not establish lower runtime.
infographic.paper_title: A locking-free enriched linearized neural network for linear elasticity

title: Helices at Twisted Ferroelectric Interfaces
authors: Kristina Holsgrove, Ronan Lynch, Conor McCluskey, Eoin Moynihan, Andrew Rogers, Xinxin Hu
abstract: We report that twisted interfaces, formed between two ferroelectric lithium niobate single crystals, contain arrays of coherently bonded and elastically deformed nanoscale structural helices, separated from one another by screw dislocations. The helices generate remarkable contrast in four dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D STEM) and through related differential phase contrast (DPC). Such images have been successfully rationalised by modelling the trajectory of electrons that channel along helical pathways as they traverse the interface, but the structural helices implied have also been directly imaged using electron ptychography. Importantly, as lithium niobate is a uniaxial ferroelectric, the torsional strain in these structural helices necessarily also causes dipolar helices to form, inferred through consideration of pertinent piezoelectric tensors and flexoelectric coefficients. Helices are topologically distinct from the more commonly reported vortices and, importantly, they are chiral. Helical (and hence chiral) character was confirmed by observing that DPC images were identical before and after the sample was inverted. Chirality was also established through second harmonic optical circularly-polarised dichroism measurements, in which unusually large interfacial signals were seen. It must be stressed that the arrays of helices observed are distinct from moiré patterns; they facilitate lattice rotation combining plastic and elastic deformation and are not simply a superposition of lattices, twisted with respect to one another. Thus, intimately bonded twisted oxide interfaces will have distinctly different characteristics from those of twisted stacks of two-dimensional van der Waals materials, opening up a new and distinct kind of twistronics.

infographic.key_insight: Twisted, coherently bonded lithium niobate interfaces form nanoscale structural helices separated by screw dislocations, with torsional strain implying chiral dipolar helices rather than simple moiré patterns.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Coupled elastic deformation, dislocations and ferroelectric polarization offer a route to chiral oxide interfaces and a distinct form of twistronics.
method: Map interfacial contrast using 4D STEM and differential phase contrast imaging.
Model electron channeling along helical pathways and directly image structural helices using electron ptychography.
Assess chirality through sample-inversion imaging and second-harmonic optical circular dichroism.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports directly imaged structural helices, unchanged DPC images after sample inversion and unusually large interfacial optical dichroism signals.
infographic.watch_item: Dipolar helices are inferred from electromechanical coupling rather than directly imaged, and device-level performance is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Helices at Twisted Ferroelectric Interfaces

title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations
authors: Yuan Qiu, Wolfgang Dahmen, Peng Chen
abstract: Physics-informed operator learning trains neural operators on the residual of a parametric partial differential equation (PDE) instead of labeled solution data, but its reliability depends on a variationally correct residual: one that is equivalent to the error in a norm dictated by the equation, the PDE-compliant norm. For nonlinear equations written as first-order systems, we prove that the first-order system least-squares residual is equivalent to the error in this norm near a solution branch if the linearized residual is stable and the residual derivative is Lipschitz continuous, possibly in a norm stronger than the error norm. We verify these conditions for monotone reaction, solution- and gradient-dependent diffusion, and compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity. The stability mechanisms vary across these classes, as do the regions where the equivalence holds, from arbitrary bounded sets to a neighborhood of the branch. In a conforming finite element space, we show that the loss excess of a state near the finite element solution is equivalent to its squared distance from that solution. We use this loss to train a reduced basis neural operator with values in this space, with solution snapshots needed only for the basis and the loss and its symbolically derived gradient assembled by the finite element library. At inference, this loss estimates the error. Numerically, the square root of the loss excess tracks the error within factors comparable to those of the linear case, and the operator achieves higher accuracy in the PDE-compliant norm than grid-based baselines evaluated in the same finite element space.

infographic.key_insight: A variationally correct first-order least-squares residual makes physics-informed operator learning locally error-equivalent in the norm dictated by the nonlinear PDE.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For nonlinear mechanics, including compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity, the training loss can provide a physically grounded error indicator at inference.
method: Establish residual–error equivalence using linearized stability and Lipschitz continuity of the residual derivative.
Train a reduced-basis neural operator in a conforming finite element space, using solution snapshots only to construct the basis.
Assemble the residual loss and its symbolically derived gradient with a finite element library.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests show that the square root of loss excess tracks error within factors comparable to the linear case, while the operator outperforms grid-based baselines in the PDE-compliant norm.
infographic.watch_item: Error equivalence is conditional and may hold only near a solution branch; its validity region depends on the PDE class.
infographic.paper_title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations

title: A GPU Interior-Point Solver with Macro-Element Condensation for Equilibrium-Based Plasticity
authors: Youssef Essousy, Mohammed-Khalil Ferradi
abstract: Equilibrium-based conic formulations of elastoplasticity and limit analysis provide statically admissible stress fields but generate large Newton systems whose sparse factorization limits three-dimensional computations. This work develops and analyzes a macro-element condensation tailored to the Newton systems arising from primal--dual interior-point methods. Exploiting four-tetrahedron macro-elements, the method eliminates stress directions and macro-internal traction-continuity multipliers, yielding reduced systems that can be solved using positive-definite factorizations, with estimated reductions of approximately \(4\times\) in dimension and structural nonzeros relative to stress-only elimination. The validity of this elimination is established through global and macro-local nonsingularity conditions. Local nonsingularity is independent of the yield criterion in elastoplasticity, whereas in limit analysis it holds directly for Rankine and is ensured for von Mises through trace-bound augmentation. Numerical results show that, relative to stress-only elimination, the proposed condensation achieves CPU speedups of up to approximately \(2\times\) and reduces peak linear-solver memory by up to \(66.5\%\). We further develop a CUDA Fortran implementation that exploits uniform macro-local blocks through batched routines and uses cuDSS for the reduced sparse solve. This implementation achieves speedups of up to \(13.5\times\) over its CPU counterpart and up to \(87.5\times\) over MOSEK, while successfully solving the largest tested 3D problems that exceed the device-memory capacity of the GPU solver CuClarabel. For elastoplasticity, we also propose a preconditioned conjugate-gradient solver that reduces device-memory requirements relative to the direct GPU solver, at the expense of increased solution time.

infographic.key_insight: Four-tetrahedron macro-element condensation shrinks interior-point Newton systems for equilibrium-based plasticity, enabling faster and more memory-efficient 3D solves.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach makes larger elastoplasticity and limit-analysis simulations feasible while retaining statically admissible stress fields.
method: Eliminate stress directions and macro-internal traction-continuity multipliers to form reduced systems compatible with positive-definite factorization.
Establish global and macro-local nonsingularity conditions, using trace-bound augmentation for von Mises limit analysis.
Use CUDA Fortran batched routines and cuDSS, with a lower-memory preconditioned conjugate-gradient option for elastoplasticity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported tests show up to 2× CPU speedup and 66.5% lower peak linear-solver memory versus stress-only elimination; the GPU implementation reaches up to 13.5× speedup over its CPU counterpart and 87.5× over MOSEK.
infographic.watch_item: The lower-memory iterative GPU solver increases solution time, and von Mises limit analysis requires trace-bound augmentation to ensure local nonsingularity.
infographic.paper_title: A GPU Interior-Point Solver with Macro-Element Condensation for Equilibrium-Based Plasticity

title: Controlling the Humanoid Robot H1-2 With a Simulated Biologically Plausible Network
authors: Fatima Atwi, Constant Roux, Christian Bergaud, Olivier Stasse
abstract: Artificial Spiking Neural Networks have gained remarkable attention in the last few years due to their proven ability in simulating biological neural cultures and producing similar activity and trends. Nevertheless, whether they can be trained for humanoid locomotion while retaining biological plausibility and robust performance at once remains an open question. We study this problem by proposing a biologically inspired spiking network, trained by different learning schemes and tested on the H1-2 Unitree Humanoid. These schemes differ in how recurrent weights are trained. Ordered from most to least biologically faithful, they are: a fixed reservoir mimicking an in-vitro neural culture, where recurrent weights are kept frozen and only a linear readout is trained, the same network but with its synapses trained by reward-modulated spike timing dependent plasticity and eligibility propagation, and finally backpropagation through time as a non biological baseline for comparison. All schemes relied on distillation of a reinforcement learning expert policy with dataset aggregation. We show that e-prop reached 100% survival rate matching backpropagation through time, whereas both the fixed reservoir and the reward-modulated STDP, though the closest to biological cultures, plateaued at a much lower performance (~43.7% and ~11% survival). We explore in further detail which trends a real culture could and could not produce until now. Finally we demonstrate brief bipedal stepping on a full size humanoid H1-2.

infographic.key_insight: A biologically inspired spiking network trained with e-prop achieved 100% survival in evaluation, matching backpropagation through time while more biologically faithful alternatives performed substantially worse.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study informs humanoid locomotion controller design by quantifying trade-offs between biological plausibility and control performance.
method: Distill a reinforcement learning expert policy using dataset aggregation.
Compare frozen recurrent weights, reward-modulated STDP, e-prop, and backpropagation through time.
Evaluate locomotion performance and demonstrate brief stepping on a full-size Unitree H1-2.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported survival rates were 100% for e-prop and backpropagation through time, approximately 43.7% for the fixed reservoir, and approximately 11% for reward-modulated STDP.
infographic.watch_item: Brief hardware stepping does not establish sustained real-world locomotion robustness, and the abstract does not specify survival-test conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Controlling the Humanoid Robot H1-2 With a Simulated Biologically Plausible Network

title: High-Order Area-Preserving Runge--Kutta Methods for Surface Diffusion Flow of Curves
authors: Lei Cui, Gengen Zhang
abstract: We propose a class of high-order area-preserving Runge--Kutta (RK) methods for the surface diffusion flow of curves, a curvature-driven geometric flow that decreases the perimeter while conserving the enclosed area. By coupling the parametric finite element approximation of the classical BGN formulation with symplectic RK time discretisation, we rigorously prove that the fully discrete scheme unconditionally conserves the enclosed area of curves. This conservation arises solely from the intrinsic symplectic structure of the RK methods, without introducing any additional constraints, auxiliary variables, or Lagrange multipliers to enforce structure preservation. To attain high temporal accuracy, we adopt $q$-stage Gauss RK methods, which are symplectic and yield order $2q$ (e.g., $q=1,2,3$). The resulting fully implicit, strongly nonlinear system is solved efficiently via an equivalent discrete formulation combined with a monolithic damped Newton iteration. Extensive numerical tests on various evolving curves validate the theoretical findings, confirming exact area preservation, high-order temporal convergence, and favorable mesh quality, while the Newton iteration count rapidly decreases to fewer than 8 per step, demonstrating the robustness of the tailored solver.

infographic.key_insight: Coupling parametric finite elements with symplectic Runge–Kutta methods yields high-order curve evolution with provably exact enclosed-area conservation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports accurate simulation of area-conserving interface relaxation driven by surface diffusion.
method: Discretize the classical BGN formulation using parametric finite elements.
Apply q-stage Gauss Runge–Kutta integration for temporal order 2q without added conservation constraints.
Solve the fully implicit nonlinear system using an equivalent formulation and monolithic damped Newton iteration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on various evolving curves confirm exact area preservation, high-order temporal convergence, and favorable mesh quality, with Newton iteration counts rapidly falling below 8 per step.
infographic.watch_item: Each time step requires a strongly nonlinear implicit solve, and the abstract does not establish unconditional discrete perimeter decrease.
infographic.paper_title: High-Order Area-Preserving Runge--Kutta Methods for Surface Diffusion Flow of Curves

title: From AI Surrogate to Engineering Tool: Toward Production Use of Fiber-Orientation Prediction in Crash CAE
authors: Osamu Ito, Yoshikazu Nakagawa, Tomoaki Tatsukawa
abstract: Crash simulations of glass-fiber-reinforced plastic parts are highly sensitive to the fiber-orientation field supplied to the material model. In conventional workflows, that field comes from resin-flow analysis, which requires molding-specialist support and takes about 25 hours of work per part. We previously proposed a surrogate model that addresses this bottleneck by predicting the orientation field in about 3 minutes. This paper reports the implementation, validation, and operational design that turned the model into an engineering tool for Honda design workflows. We present staged validation from 2D plates to production parts, evaluation against a predefined engineering angular-error criterion, and the expert review that approved design use in March 2025; the system has since been transferred to the crash-safety group and is in initial, limited use in directed fracture-prediction scenarios. The developed system combines injection-gate setting support for cases in which gates are unknown (90% gate-count accuracy, mean position error 11% of flow length), voxelization, surrogate inference, automatic mapping to the crash CAE model, and report generation in a single GUI. The complete orientation-preparation workflow takes about 0.1 hours, a 99.6% reduction from the conventional 25-hour flow-analysis route, and can be run directly by crash CAE engineers without molding-specialist support. As evidence of practical impact, component-level crash analysis using the predicted orientation field reduced the absolute peak-force error from 19.0% with an isotropic baseline to 11.4%, while confining predicted fracture to the test-observed region. The deployment lesson is that a surrogate model alone is not enough for practical adoption: gate-setting support, automatic data conversion, and shareable reporting are what make the model usable as a design tool.

infographic.key_insight: An integrated AI fiber-orientation tool reduces preparation time for crash CAE from 25 hours to 0.1 hours—a 99.6% reduction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Crash CAE engineers can prepare orientation-dependent material inputs without molding-specialist support, improving fracture and peak-force prediction over an isotropic baseline.
method: Support injection-gate setting when gates are unknown.
Voxelize geometry, infer fiber orientation, and automatically map results to the crash CAE model.
Integrate report generation in a GUI and validate from 2D plates to production parts.
infographic.evidence_signal: Staged validation used a predefined angular-error criterion; in a component crash analysis, absolute peak-force error fell from 19.0% to 11.4%, with predicted fracture confined to the test-observed region.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment remains initial and limited to directed fracture-prediction scenarios; broader applicability is not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: From AI Surrogate to Engineering Tool: Toward Production Use of Fiber-Orientation Prediction in Crash CAE

title: Alloying effects on the interface cohesion of grain boundaries in the Ni--Fe--Cr system
authors: Aljoscha Felix Baumann, Reyhaneh Ghassemizadeh, Daniel F. Urban
abstract: Grain boundaries (GBs) in polycrystalline Ni-based alloys strongly influence mechanical strength and fracture behavior, yet the effect of alloying elements such as Fe and Cr on GB cohesion remains difficult to quantify systematically. Using density functional theory (DFT), we compute rigid-body separation (RBS) curves for six symmetric-tilt Ni GBs, extracting the work of separation $W_{\mathrm{sep}}$ and maximum traction $σ_{\max}$ via the universal binding energy relation (UBER). We find that substitution of Cr or Fe into the GB plane increases both quantities relative to pure Ni GBs. To overcome the size limitations of DFT, we compare several machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP) foundation models against the DFT dataset and identify a model achieving quantitative agreement with DFT for $W_{\mathrm{sep}}$ and $σ_{\max}$. This MLIP enables systematic sampling of alloying configurations at finer concentration steps. We show that alloying-induced changes in GB cohesion depend on both, element type and local structures, revealing trends that are inaccessible with DFT alone. Extending the analysis to a ternary $\mathrm{Ni}_{56}\mathrm{Fe}_{20}\mathrm{Cr}_{24}$ composition, inspired by the principal constituents of the widely used commercial Alloy 718, shows that the binary trends provide a useful basis for interpreting the combined effect of both substitutes, while explicit ternary calculations are required to capture their interplay quantitatively. Together, these results provide a validated workflow for quantifying the effect of alloying elements on GB cohesion in multicomponent alloys. The resulting values may serve as input for continuum-scale fracture models, paving the way toward atomistically informed multiscale modeling.

infographic.key_insight: Fe or Cr substitution at Ni grain-boundary planes increases cohesion, with strengthening governed by element type and local atomic structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Atomistically predicted separation energies and peak tractions can inform continuum fracture models for multicomponent Ni-based alloys.
method: Compute DFT rigid-body separation curves for six symmetric-tilt Ni grain boundaries.
Extract work of separation and maximum traction using the universal binding energy relation.
Benchmark ML interatomic potentials against DFT, then sample finer alloy concentrations and ternary configurations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports quantitative agreement between one tested ML potential and DFT for both cohesion metrics, enabling expanded sampling including Ni56Fe20Cr24.
infographic.watch_item: Binary alloying trends do not quantitatively capture Fe–Cr interplay; explicit ternary calculations remain necessary.
infographic.paper_title: Alloying effects on the interface cohesion of grain boundaries in the Ni--Fe--Cr system

title: Axion: A differentiable, GPU-native finite element framework,demonstrated on phase-field fracture
authors: Wei Wang, Meenu Krishnan U., Somdatta Goswami
abstract: We introduce Axion (Autodifferentiable, XLA-compiled, Implicit, On-device Numerics), a differentiable, GPU-native finite element framework written in JAX. The element kernels, Newton and Krylov iterations, bound-constrained updates, staggered coupling of fields, and the loop over load increments are expressed as a single program that is just-in-time compiled and executed on the GPU without host intervention. Consistent tangent operators are obtained by forward-mode automatic differentiation of the element residual, and derivatives of the discrete solution with respect to model parameters are obtained by differentiating the same program. Global operators are applied element by element without assembling a sparse matrix, octree mesh refinement is performed within fixed-size arrays, and a cell-based domain decomposition runs the same program on several GPUs. Phase-field fracture is implemented as the first module because it combines fine mesh resolution, bound-constrained damage, and repeated nonlinear solves over a loading history, which together make it computationally expensive. On two- and three-dimensional single-edge-notched tension benchmarks, a uniformly refined Axion computation completes faster than the corresponding adaptive FEniCSx computation. At identical discretization, the two-dimensional benchmark runs 37.9 times faster on one GPU than a FEniCSx implementation on one CPU. Strong and weak scaling efficiencies on four GPUs are 92% and 96%, respectively. Large-scale demonstrations include hydraulic fracture in a poroelastic medium (0.38M degrees of freedom), fracture of a multi-material premolar under contact loading (0.69M degrees of freedom), and a concrete gravity dam (96M degrees of freedom) on a single GPU. The implementation is available as open-source software.

infographic.key_insight: Axion compiles differentiable finite element simulations into a GPU-resident program, accelerating phase-field fracture analysis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework enables large-scale fracture simulations and parameter sensitivities for coupled mechanics applications.
method: JAX/XLA compiles element kernels, nonlinear solvers, damage updates, and loading loops for GPU execution without host intervention.
Forward-mode automatic differentiation provides consistent element tangents; differentiating the simulation provides parameter sensitivities.
Matrix-free operators, fixed-array octree refinement, and cell-based domain decomposition support large and multi-GPU simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 37.9× speedup over single-CPU FEniCSx at identical 2D discretization, 92% strong and 96% weak scaling efficiency on four GPUs, and a 96M-degree-of-freedom dam simulation on one GPU.
infographic.watch_item: The reported speedup compares GPU and CPU implementations, so it should not be interpreted as a hardware-independent algorithmic advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Axion: A differentiable, GPU-native finite element framework,demonstrated on phase-field fracture

title: A time-domain adversarial example demonstrating the failure of $H^1$ elements in $a$-$φ$ electromagnetic simulation
authors: Timothy Carlson, Sanjay Govindjee
abstract: Frequently, $H^1$ continuous finite elements are used in computational electromagnetics despite it being widely known that such an interpolation is not guaranteed to furnish reliable approximations of solutions to general initial/boundary value problems. It is mathematically more natural to use $H(\text{Curl})$ elements (edge elements) than $H^1$ elements, since the former form part of a discrete complex that respects the differential-geometric structure of Maxwell's equations while the latter do not. However, most work discussing the failure of $H^1$ elements for electromagnetics is esoteric and concrete examples demonstrating the clear advantage of edge elements are generally restricted to quasi-static, frequency-domain, or eigenvalue problems. In this work, we summarize essential facts regarding $H^1$ and $H(\text{Curl})$ elements and present a physically feasible yet intentionally adversarial time-domain eddy-current example demonstrating the failure of gauge-penalized $H^1$ elements in an $a$-$φ$ formulation compared to gauge-free mixed scalar/edge $H^1/H(\text{Curl})$ elements. The results indicate that edge elements can be used to furnish reasonable results for general loading conditions, whereas penalized $H^1$ elements fail (e.g., converge to an incorrect state) even with mesh refinement.

infographic.key_insight: In an adversarial time-domain eddy-current example, gauge-penalized H¹ elements can converge to an incorrect state, while mixed H¹/H(Curl) elements yield reasonable results.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Electromagnetic simulations should use compatible finite element spaces, because mesh refinement alone may not correct errors from an unsuitable discretization.
method: Review H¹ and H(Curl) elements and their compatibility with Maxwell’s equations.
Construct a physically feasible, adversarial time-domain eddy-current problem in the a–φ formulation.
Compare gauge-penalized H¹ elements with gauge-free mixed scalar/edge H¹/H(Curl) elements under mesh refinement.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports persistent failure of penalized H¹ elements under mesh refinement, contrasted with reasonable results from edge elements, but provides no quantitative error metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The demonstration uses an intentionally adversarial problem; it does not establish failure for every H¹-based electromagnetic simulation.
infographic.paper_title: A time-domain adversarial example demonstrating the failure of $H^1$ elements in $a$-$φ$ electromagnetic simulation

title: Nonlocal regularization of sharp-crack energetics: a variational bridge from Griffith geometry to emergent constitutive degradation
authors: Qing Cheng, Yuqi Sun, Xuejun Xu
abstract: We develop a variational diffuse-crack model based on nonlocal averaging of tensile strain energy. A bounded potential acts on the scaled average, while the compressive energy remains local. The initial slope preserves the averaged tensile strain-energy density to leading order. The first variation yields a constitutive stress in which the tensile contribution is multiplied by the adjoint average of the derivative of the saturation potential. The resulting degradation is therefore determined by the stored-energy functional, without introducing an independent fracture field or prescribing a separate degradation law. For fixed smooth displacement fields with bounded strain, the energy density converges to the classical elastic strain-energy density as the averaging radius tends to zero. The Griffith surface-energy coefficient is recovered for planar opening transitions. A structure-preserving scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) scheme satisfies an exact discrete balance between the modified-energy increment and external work. We compare SAV and velocity-Verlet solutions for dynamic crack branching and Kalthoff--Winkler impact.

infographic.key_insight: Nonlocal averaging of tensile strain energy produces constitutive degradation directly from a variational energy functional, without an independent fracture field or prescribed degradation law.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework connects diffuse-crack simulation to Griffith fracture energetics while retaining a local treatment of compressive energy.
method: Apply a bounded saturation potential to scaled, nonlocally averaged tensile strain energy.
Derive tensile stress degradation through the adjoint averaging operator and the potential derivative.
Use a scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) scheme with an exact discrete modified-energy/work balance.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports recovery of classical elastic energy for fixed smooth, bounded-strain fields as the averaging radius vanishes, recovery of the Griffith coefficient for planar openings, and SAV–velocity-Verlet comparisons for dynamic branching and Kalthoff–Winkler impact.
infographic.watch_item: Recovery of the Griffith coefficient for planar openings does not by itself establish convergence for arbitrary evolving crack geometries.
infographic.paper_title: Nonlocal regularization of sharp-crack energetics: a variational bridge from Griffith geometry to emergent constitutive degradation

title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions
authors: Yue Yu, Jihong Wang, Stewart Silling, Ziwei Yang
abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can capture the nanoscale physics of fracture at the atomistic level, but their computational cost prohibits predictions at the length scales and time scales needed for many applications. Machine learning approaches, on the other hand, have been proposed as heuristic surrogates for material fracture, yet they cannot guarantee the physical consistency of the predicted response. To address this shortcoming, we propose the mesoscale neural operator (MNO): a data-driven nonlocal constitutive model that is learned directly from MD loading and displacement data. After training, it can be used in continuum fracture simulations on much larger domains and grid sizes. The key idea of the MNO is to exploit the built-in characteristic length of a nonlocal model, called the horizon, to travel across scales. Physical consistency across scales is obtained by building two structural ingredients into the MNO: a normalized kernel that renders the strain energy density invariant under horizon rescaling, and a rescaled critical bond stretch that keeps the energy release rate consistent across scales. Through tests on synthetic data, we show that the MNO and its learning workflow indeed discover the nonlocal continuum multiscale model in the form of the nonlocal kernel and the nonlinear constitutive relation. We then apply the framework to coarse-grained MD data and find that in a test problem, the learned model matches the MD strain energy density and critical energy release rate within 3%. It also predicts the peak transmitted forces within 6% in out-of-distribution tension tests. As a further demonstration, the model is applied to a plate with 4000 times the area of the training specimens and containing an initial defect. In this problem, the model reproduces the main features of dynamic brittle fracture, including branch and cascading branch networks.

infographic.key_insight: Mesoscale neural operators learn nonlocal constitutive laws from molecular dynamics while preserving strain energy density and fracture energy across horizon rescaling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables continuum fracture simulations on domains far larger than atomistic training specimens while retaining learned nanoscale material behavior.
method: Learn a nonlocal kernel and nonlinear constitutive relation from MD loading and displacement data.
Normalize the kernel to preserve strain energy density under horizon rescaling.
Rescale critical bond stretch to maintain a consistent energy release rate across scales.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic tests recovered the underlying nonlocal model; MD-based tests matched energy metrics within 3% and out-of-distribution peak forces within 6%, with fracture branching demonstrated on a plate 4,000 times the training-specimen area.
infographic.watch_item: The reported tests do not establish generalization to other materials or loading regimes; cross-scale consistency alone does not guarantee predictive accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Mesoscale Neural Operators: Learning Nonlinear Constitutive Laws from Molecular Dynamics for Scalable Fracture Predictions

title: Locking-free numerical methods for poroelasticity optimal control problems with minimal regularities
authors: Jeonghun J. Lee
abstract: We study distributed optimal control of a linear poroelastic system in a total pressure formulation, with displacement and fluid-pressure tracking and box constraints on the source control. A mechanical Schur complement gives well-posedness at zero storage for each fixed finite Lamé parameter, without estimates that grow like the inverse storage coefficient. We discretize the state and adjoint with conforming finite elements and dG(0) time stepping, and use piecewise constant controls. Under the stated regularity assumptions and a positive lower bound on storage, we prove first-order control and state error estimates uniform as the Lamé parameter increases. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence rates, examine the dependence on the Lamé and storage coefficients, and demonstrate localized pressure control with active bounds.

infographic.key_insight: A total-pressure formulation enables locking-free poroelastic optimal control, with first-order error estimates uniform as the Lamé parameter increases when storage has a positive lower bound.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports bounded fluid-source control in nearly incompressible porous materials while tracking displacement and fluid pressure.
method: Use a mechanical Schur complement to establish zero-storage well-posedness for each fixed finite Lamé parameter.
Discretize state and adjoint with conforming finite elements and dG(0) time stepping.
Represent box-constrained source controls with piecewise constants.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments confirm predicted convergence rates, probe Lamé and storage coefficient dependence, and demonstrate localized pressure control with active bounds.
infographic.watch_item: Zero-storage well-posedness does not imply zero-storage error guarantees: the stated convergence estimates require storage bounded away from zero.
infographic.paper_title: Locking-free numerical methods for poroelasticity optimal control problems with minimal regularities
